newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: De Klerk knew of S.African covert acts, killer says.
newsitem.headline: De Klerk knew of S.African covert acts, killer says.

text.p: A convicted apartheid-era assassin said on Wednesday that F.W. de Klerk, leader of South Africa's opposition National Party, knew of covert state military units that operated while he was president.

"De Klerk cannot say he did not know that such (covert) organisations existed. He gave the order for the attack on the Transkei in 1993," Eugene de Kock told a court where he is pleading for leniency after conviction for six murders.

"Who did he think was going to carry out that attack? He certainly knew there were covert organisations," said de Kock, former commander of a secret death-squad unit run by the apartheid regime to hunt black guerrillas.

Five youngsters aged 12-17 died in an attack in 1993 on a home in the Transkei, a nominally independent homeland. The incident nearly derailed government-opposition negotiations that brought democracy the next year.
De Klerk's government insisted that at least three of the five youths were guerrillas in the Azanian People's Liberation Army (APLA), even though the movement denied it.
Soon afterwards de Klerk was jointly awarded the Nobel peace prize with Nelson Mandela who is now president. The joint award was put in doubt for a while by the attack.
De Kock also said that tonnes of documents were destroyed in cement mixer-type machines by police after reports on death squad activities started to surface.
"For days we burnt evidence," he testified. "Literally tonnes, and tonnes and tonnes of evidence was destroyed."

De Klerk apologised for apartheid last month and acknowledged that his and previous governments had approved "unconventional" actions that "created the environment within which abuses and gross violations of human rights could take place".

"Within my knowledge and experience (these actions) never included the authorisation of assassination, murder, torture, rape, assault or the like," he told a Truth and Reconciliation Commission that is trying to explain and reveal the past.
"Nor did I individually directly or indirectly ever suggest, order or authorise any such action," he added.
De Klerk could not immediately be reached for comment on the testimony by de Kock, who is hoping for a lenient sentence by showing his actions were ordered from above.
To do this he has implicated numerous senior officials from the old apartheid regime in some of the most damning revelations to date by an "insider".

De Kock said he would now rather be a member of Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) or the radical Pan Africanist Congress than support de Klerk's National Party, which he said had abandoned his unit's members.

"My opinion was that de Klerk had totally abdicated...I regard him as one of the biggest cowards in this country. He was like a small scared dog that lay on his back and just gave up," the 47-year-old career policeman said.
